passage:
Monday. Suraj was helping Pradeep with quadratic equations. "Just do the D thing, then plug into the formula, easy." He raced through three lines, using phrases like "the D thing" and "the usual trick". Pradeep nodded and said "Got it" at every step.

Wednesday. In the class quiz, Pradeep stared at the first question and left half the paper empty. Afterwards he showed Suraj the blank sheet. "I said got it. I didn't."

Saturday. Suraj tried again. What was D? What did a, b and c stand for? He solved one equation slowly and wrote down every step, then handed Pradeep the pen. Pradeep solved the next one with a single mistake, and they fixed it together.

qa.q: What did Pradeep say at every step on Monday?
qa.a: Pradeep said "Got it" at every step.

qa.q: What might Suraj have felt when Pradeep showed the blank quiz sheet?
qa.a: Surprised and guilty, realising the nodding had hidden the confusion.

qa.q: What changed in Suraj's second explanation?
qa.a: Suraj explained what D, a, b and c stood for, solved one equation slowly with every step written down, and handed Pradeep the pen.

qa.q: Why might Pradeep have kept nodding and saying "Got it"?
qa.a: Pradeep probably did not want to seem slow or hold Suraj up, so nodding felt easier than admitting confusion. 🙂

grounding: Shows a teenager skipping steps and using class shorthand while the friend nods without understanding.

passage: Vasudha, sit. I heard you got cross with your friend today, so let me tell you something about me. I'm Divyansh, your uncle, and at sixteen I was the circuit expert in class. Meera asked me to explain Ohm's law. I said, "V equals I R, just rearrange it, the usual, you know," and scribbled symbols fast. She nodded, and I felt clever. Next day she showed me her notebook: three wrong answers and question marks all over. "I nodded because everyone else gets it," she said quietly. I had skipped every step that felt obvious to me. So I took a torch battery, a bulb and a wire, and let her change one thing at a time. That afternoon she finally said, "Oh!"

qa.q: What did Divyansh say when explaining Ohm's law?
qa.a: Divyansh said, "V equals I R, just rearrange it, the usual, you know."

qa.q: How did Divyansh feel after Meera nodded?
qa.a: Clever and satisfied, thinking the explanation had worked.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Divyansh explained?
qa.a: After seeing the question marks in the notebook, Divyansh used a battery, a bulb and a wire so Meera could change one thing at a time.

qa.q: Why did Meera nod even though she did not understand?
qa.a: Meera thought everyone else understood and did not want to be the only one who did not.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how he skipped obvious steps with shorthand and a nodding friend did not understand.

passage:
Dear Ayesha,
I owe you an apology for yesterday's chemistry "help."
You asked me how to balance that equation, and I rattled off, "Just count the atoms, fix the coefficients, don't touch the subscripts, easy." Then I did three examples in about two minutes. You kept nodding, so I thought you had it.
Today in the test I saw you sitting with your pen still for ten minutes on question four. That's when I understood. You were nodding because I was going so fast you didn't know what to ask.
I forgot that a month ago I didn't know what a coefficient was either. I learned it slowly, from Ma'am, with drawings.
So can we try again on Saturday? This time you do the example, I only ask questions, and if I say a word you don't know, you stop me. I promise not to say "easy."
Your friend,
Jahnavi

qa.q: Which question did Ayesha sit on for ten minutes?
qa.a: Question four.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel watching Ayesha in the test?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt guilty and sorry, realising the nodding had hidden confusion caused by the rushed explanation.

qa.q: What is Jahnavi's plan for Saturday, and why is it better?
qa.a: Ayesha does the example while Jahnavi only asks questions, and Ayesha stops any unknown word, so understanding is checked instead of assumed.

qa.q: Why might Ayesha have kept nodding the day before?
qa.a: Ayesha was probably confused and too embarrassed to stop someone going so fast, so nodding felt easier than asking.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who explains too fast with class shorthand while a friend nods without understanding.

passage:
So, Mehta ma'am asked me to talk about peer tutoring for the school podcast. I'm Sachin, Class Eleven, and here's my big failure.
My friend Wasim missed two weeks with a fever, and I offered to catch him up on coding. I opened my laptop and went, "Okay, so you just loop through the array, increment the counter, break when you hit the condition." Twenty minutes, very fast, lots of words from class. Wasim kept saying, "Yeah, yeah, okay."
Next day's practical, he couldn't write a single loop. He told me later he didn't know what "array" meant. He hadn't wanted to look slow.
Honestly, I felt terrible. And a little annoyed, because he said yes. But then I remembered I had nodded exactly like that in Class Nine.
Second time, I drew boxes on paper. Each box a locker. No words he didn't know. He wrote his first loop in ten minutes.

qa.q: How long was Wasim away with a fever?
qa.a: Wasim missed two weeks with a fever.

qa.q: How did Sachin feel after the practical?
qa.a: Sachin felt terrible and a bit annoyed, then understood after remembering nodding the same way in Class Nine.

qa.q: What changed in Sachin's second try, and why did it work?
qa.a: Sachin drew lockers on paper and used no words Wasim didn't know, so Wasim could follow each step.

qa.q: What was it like for Wasim during the first session?
qa.a: Wasim felt lost and did not want to look slow, so he kept saying "yeah, okay" without understanding "array."

grounding: Shows a teenager who explains coding too fast with class shorthand while a friend nods without understanding.

passage:
Monday. Vishal sat with Irawati in the library to help with triangles. "It's SAS, so they're congruent, then CPCT, done." He wrote three lines. Irawati nodded twice and said, "Oh, okay." He felt pleased.
Wednesday. The class test came back. Irawati had left the whole question blank. At lunch she said quietly, "I didn't know what CPCT was. I didn't want to ask again."
Vishal went red. He had learned those letters in Class Nine and had stopped hearing them as a code.
Friday. He tried again, slower. "What do you already know about triangles?" She knew that equal sides meant something. He drew two paper triangles, cut them out and laid one on top of the other. He wrote the full words, not the letters. Then he gave her a new question and kept quiet.
She got it on the second try. "Why didn't you just say that on Monday?" she asked.

qa.q: What did Irawati leave blank in the test?
qa.a: Irawati had left the whole question blank.

qa.q: How did Vishal feel when Irawati explained why she left it blank?
qa.a: Vishal felt embarrassed and went red, realising the shorthand he used was a code she didn't know.

qa.q: What small changes made Friday work?
qa.a: Vishal started from what Irawati knew, used paper triangles and full words, then gave her a new question and stayed quiet.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt on Monday when she nodded?
qa.a: Irawati was probably confused and a little ashamed, nodding because she did not want to ask again.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who skips steps and uses class shorthand, while a friend nods without understanding, until he slows down.

passage: Siddharth, you remind me of myself at fifteen, so listen. Your Jaya Dadi was the maths girl of her class. One evening before the exam, my friend Meenal came over with her geometry book and asked me to explain circle theorems. I rattled it off: "Angle at centre is double, so this is sixty, cyclic quad, opposite angles, done." I jumped over every line in between, because to me they were plain as daylight. Meenal kept nodding, "Hmm, hmm, okay." I felt so clever. The next day she showed me her paper. The same question, left blank. She said, "I didn't want to look slow in front of you." That stung. I had forgotten that I too once stared at those circles as if they were a foreign alphabet. After that, I drew every step on paper and stopped to say, "Now you write the next line."

qa.q: What did Meenal bring when she came over?
qa.a: Meenal came over with her geometry book and asked Jaya to explain circle theorems.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel while explaining, and how did that change the next day?
qa.a: Jaya felt clever and pleased while rattling off the answer, then stung and guilty on seeing Meenal's blank paper.

qa.q: What could young Jaya have done that evening to be sure Meenal understood?
qa.a: Jaya could have drawn each step, said why it followed, and asked Meenal to write the next line herself instead of trusting the nods.

qa.q: What was the lesson like for Meenal?
qa.a: For Meenal it was confusing and a little embarrassing; she nodded because she did not want to look slow, and then could not answer that question in the exam.

grounding: Shows a teenager explaining too fast with class shorthand while a friend nods along without understanding.
